## Background

### General Background
Genomics is the study of an organism's complete genetic material, or genome. Rather than focusing on single genes, genomics investigates the gene function and interactions across the entire genome of an organism. Advances in sequencing technologies allow researchers to generate short or long DNA sequences called reads, which are further assembled to construct more complete genome sequence. Following genome assembly, the resulting sequence can be compared against reference genome to derive genes or variants of biological importance. Further, genome annotation is performed to identify genomic features and  their functions. It includes structural annotation, which locates genes and other genomic components, as well as functional annotation, which assigns potential functions to existing genes by comparing them with known biological databases. This can help researchers to investigate the physiological functions of genes as well as identify metabolic pathways involved in biological processes, including production of metabolites that may contribute to microbial interactions. Furthermore, increasing the number of annotated genes in microorganisms such as yeasts can help researchers understand molecular mechanisms behind biocontrol activity. 
Microbial interactions play significant role in maintaining plant health because certain microorganisms can inhibit the growth of plant pathogens. In sustainable agricultural systems, biological control or bio-control uses beneficial organism or their metabolites to prevent or inhibit disease or pathogen causing disease. This practice has gained substantial attention as it does not involve use of chemicals to control the pathogenic effect. Among the microorganisms studied for biological control, yeasts have shown biocontrol potential through multiple mechanisms, including competition for nutrients and space, secretion of enzymes, toxin production and production of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). 
VOCs are small, volatile molecules with low water solubility and high vapor pressure. Example include ethanol, 3-methyl-1-butanol and 2-phenylethanol (alcohols) as well s ethyl acetate and isoamyl acetate (esters). Yeast species can vary in these chemicals' relative quantity and composition. The production of VOCs in yeasts is associated with several metabolic pathways such as Ehrlich pathway and ester biosynthesis. These pathways are catalyzed by specific enzymes that convert biochemical precursors such as metabolites into volatile organic compounds, such as alcohols and esters. Variations in genes encoding these enzymes may contribute to differences in VOC-producing potential among different yeast strains.

### Project-Specific Background

## Methods

## Sequencing Data and Provenance
Genomic DNA was extracted from two wild yeast isolates: Wickerhamomyces anomalus NK1 and Hanseniaspora uvarum AD. Before sequencing, the isolated DNA was checked for quality and prepared for library prepration. This involves repairing DNA or attaching adapters that help DNA sequence interact with Oxford Nanopore sequencing system. The prepared DNA library is loaded onto a flow cell with nanopores embedded in its membrane. Next, the ONT sequencing system detects and records the changes in ionic current caused by DNA molecules passing through nanopores. These electrical signals are converted to nucleotide sequences by basecalling software to generate FASTQ files containing sequence reads and their respective quality scores.
For this project, we were directly provided FASTQ files generated from Oxford Nanopore long-read sequencing in two separate years (2025 and 2026) for both yeast isolates. As a result, combined FASTQ files (WA_final.fastq and HU_final.fastq) were used to provide more sequencing data and greater genome coverage for further donwstream analyses.

## Quality Assessment and read filtering
The quality of Oxford Nanopore sequencing reads can vary, with read quality decreasing towards the end of individual reads. Therefore, assessing read quality before genome assembly and subsequent downstream analyses is an important step. Quality control was performed using Sequali (version 1.0.2), which was installed and executed in a dedicated Conda environment (sequali-env). The FASTQ files were provided as input to generate HTML reports containing sequencing statistics, including read length distribution, N50, mean read length, Q-scores and relative adapter contamination.

Following the quality assessment, Filtlong (v0.3.1) was used to filter the long sequencing reads. Filtlong was installed and implemented in separate Conda environment (filtong_env). The --keep_percent 75 parameter was used to retain the best 75 % of reads based on its quality and length ranking. The resulting filtered FASTQ files were reassessed using Sequali to inspect changes in sequencing quality as well as compare the data with the original FASTQ files. These filtered FASTQ files were used to construct genome assembly.

## Genome Assembly
Genome assembly is the process of aligning and merging millions of fragmented DNA reads to reconstruct continuous genome sequence. Flye (2.9.6-bi802), a de novo assembler was installed and implemented in new Conda environment (flye_env) to complete genome assembly. The --nano-raw parameter tells Flye that the input reads are raw Oxford Nanopore sequencing reads. Flye was aimed at locating overlaps, constructing genome graph, resolve genomic structures and generate contigs for subsequent analysis.

## Genome Polishing
The resulting contigs from genome assembly may contain errors due to imprecisions in long-read sequencing. Genome polishing involves comparing the original sequencing reads against the assembled contigs to identify and rectify potential errors in the consensus sequence. Two rounds of polishing were performed using Medaka (version 2.2.1) to achieve accurate genome assemblies. Medaka was equipped and executed in a separate Conda environment (medaka_final). The first round of Medaka was performed on assembled FASTA files and corresponding sequencing reads. The second round of polishing was conducted over polished files from Medaka round 1 and respective sequencing reads to further refine the consensus sequence.

## Assembly Quality Assessment
Assembly quality was assessed with QUAST 5.3.0 (Quality Assessment tool for Genome Assemblies). It generates assembly statistics such as N50, number of contigs, total assembly length and contig length distribution to evaluate resultant assembly. QUAST was used with reference sequence to compare flye assembly against reference sequence.
Genome completeness was assessed using BUSCO v6.0.0_cv1 (Benchmarking Universal Single-Copy Orthologs). It generates reports with BUSCO score displaying complete, duplicated, fragmented or missing genes to provide an approximation of assembly completeness.

## Genome Annotation
Genome Annotation involves structural annotation as well as functional annotation performed using tools funannotate (v1.8.15) and eggNOG-mapper respectively. Structural annotation is the process of identifying the physical coordinates of genomic features—such as protein-coding genes (Open Reading Frames, exons, introns, coding sequences/CDS), tRNAs, and repetitive elements—along your contigs. funannotate is a fungal genome annotation pipeline that integrates both strategies to build a high-confidence consensus set of gene models. funannotate runs multiple ab initio predictors (such as Augustus and GeneMark-ES/ET) alongside protein and transcript alignments. Where the tools disagree, funannotate uses EvidenceModeler (EVM)—a weighted scoring system—to select the most biologically supported gene structure, prioritizing physical evidence over statistical guesses.
Functional annotation assigns biochemical, cellular, and metabolic roles to those predicted proteins. To infer protein function computationally, we compare unknown sequences against databases of characterized proteins.eggNOG-mapper (emapper.py) aligns your query proteins against pre-computed evolutionary trees in the EggNOG database, places each protein into a fine-grained Orthologous Group (OG), and transfers functional annotations strictly from verified orthologs.
